title: Navigating the Terminal: pwd, ls, cd
lead: See where you are, get to know your surroundings, reach your target: move around the file system safely with `pwd`, `ls` and `cd`.
objectives: You see your current directory with `pwd` and know that the `~` in the prompt is the home directory.
You list directory contents with `ls` and its options (`-l`, `-a`, `-h`) and find hidden files.
You move between directories with `cd` using the shortcuts `~`, `-`, `..` and `.`.
You know the difference between absolute and relative paths, read the columns in `ls -l` output and use Tab completion.

sections.title: Where am I? pwd and the home directory
body: In Linux everything lives in a single tree whose root is `/`. In the terminal you are always somewhere in this tree: your **current working directory**. Most commands act there unless told otherwise.
`pwd` (print working directory) prints your current directory as a **full path**. A command run in the wrong directory can cause data loss, so check with `pwd` especially before deleting or copying.
When you log in you land in your **home directory**, such as `/home/student`. It is written `~` for short; that is the `~` in the prompt.

commands.what: Shows your current directory as a full path.
commands.where: Before any operation, especially deleting and copying.
commands.why: Prevents wrong operations in the wrong directory.

commands.what: Prints the expansion of the `~` shortcut, i.e. the full path of your home directory.
commands.where: When you want to know the path of your home directory.
commands.why: `~` is expanded by the shell; commands see the real path.

sections.tip: A `~` in the prompt means you are in your home directory; in any other directory only the last folder name, such as `Documents`, is shown.

sections.title: What is inside? ls
body: `ls` lists the contents of your current directory. If you give it a directory as a path, it lists that one without entering it: `ls /etc`. Look first, then decide.
Options start with `-` and can be combined: `-l` detailed list, `-a` including hidden files, `-h` human-readable sizes (K, M, G). `ls -lah` gives all three at once.

commands.what: Lists the files and folders in your current directory.
commands.where: After entering a directory or when checking whether something exists.
commands.why: Working where you don't know what is there is dangerous.

commands.what: Lists the contents of the given directory without entering it.
commands.why: You look without changing your working directory.

commands.what: Also shows hidden files whose names start with a dot.
commands.why: Hidden files do not appear in normal `ls` output.

commands.what: Detailed list; prints sizes as K/M/G.

sections.tip: If `ls` output is long in a directory with many files, use `ls -l | head` to see the first lines.

sections.title: Reach your target: cd
body: `cd` (change directory) changes your working directory. On success it prints nothing; you see the result in the prompt or with `pwd`. If the directory does not exist, you get an error.

Shortcuts: `cd` (without an argument) and `cd ~` take you to your home directory, `cd ..` goes up one directory, `cd -` returns to the previous directory. `.` is the current directory; `cd .` stays where you are.
Case matters: `Documents` and `documents` are different names. If a name contains a space, use quotes: `cd "My Files"`.

commands.what: Enters the `Documents` folder in your current directory.
commands.where: When going down into a subfolder.
commands.why: Relative path: starts from where you are.
`..` points to the parent directory in every directory.

commands.what: Returns to the previous directory and prints its path.
commands.where: When switching back and forth between two directories.
commands.why: Saves you from retyping long paths.

commands.what: Typed without an argument, goes to the home directory.

sections.tip: If you get lost, type `cd`, then check with `pwd`: you are back in your home directory.

sections.title: Absolute and relative paths
body: An **absolute path** starts with `/` and is the full address from the root: `/usr/bin`. It always leads to the same place regardless of where you are. `~/Documents` also counts as absolute, because `~` expands to a full path.

A **relative path** does not start with `/` and is computed from your current directory: `Documents`, `../Downloads`, `./notes.txt`. The same spelling leads to different places in different directories.
`..` is the parent directory and `.` is the current directory; they can be chained: `cd ../..` goes up two directories. When you are in `/usr/bin`, `cd ../..` takes you to the root `/`.

commands.what: Goes straight to `/usr/bin` using an absolute path.
commands.where: When heading to a target regardless of where you are.
commands.why: The result is always the same.

commands.where: When leaving a deep folder quickly.
commands.why: In relative paths `..` can be chained.

sections.tip: If you are unsure, type the absolute path; for short distances a relative path is faster.

sections.title: Hidden files
body: Files and folders whose names **start with a dot** are hidden: `.bashrc`, `.profile`, `.config`. Normal `ls` does not show them, `ls -a` does. Settings are usually kept in these files.
In `ls -a` output you see two special entries: `.` (the current directory) and `..` (the parent directory). They are not real files but shortcuts present in every directory.

commands.what: Lists everything in the home directory, including hidden files.
commands.why: Files like `.bashrc` only show up this way.

commands.where: For a cleaner list (on a real VM).
commands.why: Same as `-a`, but without the two shortcut entries.

sections.warn: Do not delete or damage configuration files such as `.bashrc` and `.profile`; your shell environment may break.

sections.title: Reading ls -l output
body: `ls -l` gives one line per file. Example: `-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 35 Nov 12 10:32 notes.txt`. From left to right:

**1st character:** type. `-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link. **Next 9 characters:** permissions (`rw-r--r--`: owner reads/writes, group and others read). **Number:** link count. **Two names:** owner user and group. **Number:** size in bytes. **Date:** last modification. **Last:** name.
The `total` line at the top is the sum of disk blocks used. You will see the details of permissions in later modules.

commands.what: Detailed list showing type, permissions, owner, size, date and name.
commands.where: When checking a file's owner or permissions.
commands.why: All the basic information about a file in one line.

commands.what: Shows a directory itself (not its contents) in detail.
commands.where: When checking a directory's permissions or owner.

sections.tip: If the line starts with `d` it is a folder, if it starts with `-` it is a file.

sections.title: Tab completion
body: Don't type long names by hand in the terminal: type the first letters of the name and press **Tab**. If there is a single match, the shell completes the name. If there are several matches, press Tab **twice**; the options are listed.
It works for commands as well as file and folder names. It saves time and prevents typos: if Tab does not complete, that name does not exist or you are in the wrong directory.
Extra shortcut: the **↑/↓** keys recall previous commands. These features work in a real shell (on your VM).

commands.what: Typing `Doc` and pressing Tab completes it to `Documents/`.
commands.where: In every command, when typing file and folder names.
commands.why: You type less and make fewer mistakes.

sections.tip: Make it a habit: press Tab before typing a name from start to finish.

vm.intro: Run these tasks on your own VM (Ubuntu, Rocky, Alma or WSL). They are all read-only; they change nothing.

v01.title: Where am I?
v01.text: Open the terminal; print your current directory and the path of your home directory, and paste the output.
differs: If your username is not `student`, your own name appears in the path; that is normal.
If the output is `/root`, you are running as root; switch to a normal user.

v02.title: Find hidden files
v02.text: List your home directory including hidden files and find the `.bashrc` file.
differs: You may see many hidden folders (`.cache`, `.config`); that is normal.
On WSL, `.bashrc` is still in the home directory; make sure you look under `~`.

v03.title: Absolute, relative and cd -
v03.text: Go to `/var/log` using an absolute path, go up with `..`, return with `cd -` and print the paths.

blocks.cmd:
cd /var/log
pwd
cd ..
pwd
cd -
cd /etc
pwd

differs: `cd -` also prints the previous path by itself; seeing an extra line is normal.
If `/var/log` does not exist (very minimal image), try `cd /usr/bin` instead.

v04.title: Read ls -l
v04.text: List the file `/etc/passwd` in detail; read its type, permissions, owner and size.
differs: A `.` or `+` at the end of the permissions (SELinux/ACL) is normal.
Size and date vary depending on your system.

v05.title: Tab completion
v05.text: Type `cd Doc` and press Tab without pressing Enter; it should complete to `Documents/`. Then type `cd ~/` and press Tab twice to see the list. When done, say "Done".
differs: If it does not complete, the `Documents` folder does not exist or you are not in your home directory; check with `pwd`.
On some minimal systems the `bash-completion` package is needed for completion.

options: Shows the current directory as a full path
q1.explain: `pwd` (print working directory) prints the working directory.

q2.explain: `..` is the parent directory; use `cd ~` for home and `cd -` for the previous one.

q3.q: Which one is used to see hidden files?
q3.explain: `-a` shows files whose names start with a dot.

q4.q: In `ls -l` output, what does it mean if a line starts with `d`?
q4.explain: The first character shows the type: `d` directory, `-` file, `l` symbolic link.

summary: `pwd` tells you where you are, `ls` what is there, `cd` where to go.
`~` is the home directory, `..` the parent directory, `.` the current directory, `cd -` the previous directory.
An absolute path starts with `/`; a relative path is computed from your current directory.
`ls -a` shows hidden files, `ls -l` shows type, permissions, owner, size and date.
Complete with Tab; mind upper and lower case.

glossary.meaning: The directory you are currently in, where commands run by default.
The directory that belongs to the user; abbreviated `~`, for example `/home/student`.
A full address starting from the `/` root.
A path starting from your current directory.
A file whose name starts with a dot, visible with `ls -a`.
Typing the start of a name and pressing Tab to have the shell complete it.
